reading.body:
Amazon Web Services recorded $717 billion in revenue in 2025 while operating two major AI product lines: SageMaker for full-stack ML lifecycle management and Bedrock for managed foundation model access.

AWS sits at the intersection of compute supply and AI demand. SageMaker's architecture—unified data lakes, model monitoring, bias detection, and governance tools—reflects the infrastructure required to run production AI at scale. Bedrock's API model with VPC support and IAM integration suggests AWS is positioning itself as the managed layer between foundation models and enterprise users who want isolation and control. Both products point to a company treating AI not as a feature but as a platform business spanning data, compute, and model serving.

The scale here matters for power and buildings. A $717 billion revenue company in cloud services operates data centers globally to deliver these products. The fact that SageMaker includes toxicity detection, guardrails, and data lineage tracking indicates AWS is building compliance and observability into the compute layer itself. This is not decorative. As regulatory exposure grows, the infrastructure provider that bakes governance into the platform gains advantage over those that bolt it on later.

The data does not specify AWS's capital spending, energy consumption, or data center locations. It does not break out AI revenue from total AWS revenue or show whether SageMaker and Bedrock are growing faster than legacy services. It does not name which foundation models Bedrock serves or how much compute AWS allocates to these two products versus others.

profile_text.body:
Amazon Web Services is the cloud computing arm of Amazon, and its SageMaker page presents the next generation of Amazon SageMaker as a center for data, analytics, and AI. The company describes SageMaker Unified Studio as a single development environment that unifies access to data stored in data lakes, data warehouses, and third-party or federated sources, with governance built in. The site lists SageMaker AI tools including HyperPod, JumpStart, and MLOps, along with Amazon Q Developer, which the company describes as its generative AI assistant for software development. Amazon Web Services is a public company with the ticker AMZN, CIK 0001018724, founded in 1994 and headquartered in Seattle, WA, USA. Its most recent reported revenue, on a 10-K for the period ending 2025-12-31, is $716,924,000,000.

Two AI products are tracked for the company. Amazon SageMaker is listed under Cloud AI Services and Model APIs, with full machine learning lifecycle management, model monitoring, bias detection, and explainability tools. AWS Bedrock is listed in the same category as a managed foundation model API service with IAM integration, VPC support, model evaluation tools, and AgentCore for agent orchestration. The site describes SageMaker's lakehouse architecture as unifying data across Amazon S3 data lakes and Amazon Redshift data warehouses, with Apache Iceberg-compatible tools, zero-ETL integrations, and federated query. Governance features named on the page include the Amazon SageMaker Catalog, fine-grained permissions, data classification, toxicity detection, guardrails, and responsible AI policies. Open source analytics work is described on Amazon Athena, Amazon EMR, and AWS Glue. The page quotes an unnamed automotive customer and Carrier on their use of SageMaker.

Among the litigation facts held for the company is a case, Haugland v. Anthropic PBC, in the District Court, D. Delaware. A litigation record for the company also lists 114 cases in Washington.
